turn/pair: Take two entries of a query, a pair: two and one. Drawn from the origin, the pair is an arrow, q.
turn/key: Two entries of a key, one and one, make a second arrow, k. Their dot product, two plus one, is three: their score, how well they match.
turn/spin: Now turn k about the origin. The score changes as it goes: highest when k points along q, zero at a right angle, and negative when it points away.
turn/length: Yet k never grows or shrinks. Its length, its norm, stays the same, so its tip runs round a circle. Only its direction changes.
turn/name: That is a rotation, from rota, the Latin for a wheel: the tip goes round like a point on a turning rim.
turn/quarter: So where does a turned arrow land? Start with a quarter turn, ninety degrees. Angles turn counterclockwise, against a clock's hands: from across toward up.
turn/path: Think of q as a path: two steps across, then one step up.
turn/steps: Turn the whole path a quarter turn. The two steps across now point up, and the one step up now points left. So q lands at minus one, two.
turn/swap: For any pair A, b, a quarter turn swaps the entries, then flips the sign of the new first one: minus b, A.
unit/one: Other angles need a little more. Start from the simplest arrow: length one, pointing straight across, at one, zero.
unit/tip: Turn it by an angle, say sixty degrees. Its tip stays on the circle of radius one, and lands partway up.
unit/cos: How far across it lands is the angle's cosine, written cos. Here, one half.
unit/sin: How far up is its sine, written s i n: about zero point eight seven.
unit/ninety: Turn it all the way to ninety degrees, and it points straight up: cos is zero, and sine is one.
unit/gunter: The name cosine ties the two together. In sixteen twenty, in a book of tables for angles, Edmund Gunter wrote of the sine of the complement, which for short he called the cosine.
unit/complement: The complement is what an angle lacks of a right angle: here, thirty degrees. Measured from straight up, the arrow is that far over, so its across part, one half, is the sine of thirty degrees.
unit/lookup: Like e to a power, cosines and sines are looked up, in a table or on a calculator, not worked out by hand.
rule/split: Now any pair, A and b. Like q's path, it is A steps along one, zero, then b steps along zero, one.
rule/both: Turn the path by an angle, and both kinds of step turn with it. One, zero lands at cos, sine.
rule/up: Zero, one starts a quarter turn further round, so it lands a quarter turn past cos, sine. A quarter turn swaps and flips the first sign: minus sine, cos.
rule/rule: So A, b lands at A times cos, sine, plus b times minus sine, cos. Entry by entry: A cos minus b sine, then A sine plus b cos.
rule/check: At ninety degrees, cos is zero and sine is one, so the rule gives minus b, A: the quarter turn again.
try/p: Back to the key, one, one. Where does a sixty degree turn take it? cos sixty degrees is one half, and sine sixty degrees is about zero point eight seven.
try/first: The first entry is A cos minus b sine: one times one half, minus one times zero point eight seven. About minus zero point three seven.
try/second: The second is A sine plus b cos: one times zero point eight seven, plus one times one half. About one point three seven.
try/done: So k turns to minus zero point three seven, one point three seven: a sixth of a full turn further round, and just as long as before.
